opus-5.5.text:
I think they have a genuinely strong case in a few areas. The clearest one is anything where the physics is really hard to model. With locomotion we've been lucky: rigid-body dynamics, contacts with fairly stiff terrain, motors we can characterize pretty well. Once you randomize enough parameters, the policy transfers. But as soon as you get into deformable objects, cloth, cables, food, liquids, or really rich contact like in-hand manipulation with friction that changes all the time, simulation either becomes inaccurate or so slow that you lose the main advantage, which is massive parallel throughput. If your simulator is wrong in ways you can't randomize away, learning directly on the real system starts to look very attractive.

The second point is that the real world gives you the true distribution for free. You don't have to guess what the sensor noise looks like, how the camera behaves under weird lighting, or how a particular gearbox wears down over time. With sim-to-real, a big part of the engineering effort goes into closing that gap: actuator networks, domain randomization, careful system identification. Someone training in the real world can say, "I skip all of that, and whatever I learn is by definition correct for this robot."

And third, there's fine-tuning and adaptation. Even if you pretrain in simulation, the last few percent of performance, adapting to a specific robot, a specific environment, or a task that drifts over time, is naturally a real-world problem. I think that's where real-world RL makes the most sense right now.

Where I'm more skeptical is the idea of learning everything from scratch on hardware. Sample efficiency, safety, resets, and robots breaking during exploration are still big issues, especially for dynamic systems like legged robots, where a bad action means a fall. So my view is that the strongest case for real-world learning is as a complement: use simulation to get a robust, safe starting point, then use real data to correct what the simulator got wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation limits for deformable objects and rich contact generally, but does not identify opening a cardboard box as the bottleneck in a robot box-handling task.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the strongest argument they have is the one that's hardest to engineer away: the sim-to-real gap is fundamentally a modeling problem, and some things are just very hard to model well. For legged locomotion we got lucky in a sense. Rigid-body dynamics, contacts with the ground, motor models — those are things we can simulate reasonably accurately, and where we can't, domain randomization covers a lot of the error. So for walking, I'm fairly convinced simulation is the right tool.

But the moment you move to manipulation, especially with deformable objects, soft contacts, fluids, cables, cloth, that argument gets much weaker. Simulating a towel or a plastic bag realistically enough that a policy trained on it transfers directly is still an open problem, and it may be more expensive to get the simulator right than to just collect the data in the real world. Same for perception. If your policy relies on RGB images, you now need realistic rendering, realistic lighting, realistic textures, and every detail you don't model becomes a potential failure mode. Real-world data has none of these problems; the physics are free and correct by definition.

The other point they make, which I think is fair, is about long-tail behavior. In simulation you only see what you thought to put in the simulation. The real world constantly surprises you with cases you never anticipated, and a robot learning in the real world is exposed to those by default. So if the goal is robustness to the actual deployment environment rather than to a distribution you designed, real-world learning has an honest advantage.

Where I push back is on sample efficiency and safety. Real-world RL means a robot falling over thousands of times, breaking hardware, needing a person to reset it. That's still very expensive, and most of the impressive real-world results I've seen either start from a sim-trained policy or rely on a lot of structure to keep exploration safe. So my view is that it's not really sim versus real. For the parts of the problem we can simulate, we should, because it's orders of magnitude cheaper. And then real-world fine-tuning or real-world data is how you close the remaining gap, especially in the domains where our simulators are genuinely not good enough yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation limits for manipulation generally, including deformable objects, but does not identify opening a cardboard box as the bottleneck in a mostly simulatable box-handling task.

astra-6.text:
I think they have a good case when it comes to tasks where the physics is difficult to simulate. For locomotion, we can get a reasonably good model of the robot and its interaction with the ground. But if you want to manipulate deformable objects, like folding clothes, or interact with materials whose properties you don’t know, building an accurate simulation becomes much harder.

In those cases, learning directly in the real world means you’re learning with the actual dynamics. You don’t have to solve the simulation problem first, and you don’t have that gap to cross when you deploy the policy.

The question is how much real-world experience you need, and how you collect it. Can you reset the task automatically? Can the robot explore without breaking itself or the objects around it? If you can handle those things, then real-world reinforcement learning has a strong case. I also think there’s a lot of room for combining the two: learn as much as you can in simulation, then use real-world experience to adapt to the things the simulator doesn’t capture.

r001.rationale: The response describes deformable-object manipulation and unknown material properties as difficult to simulate, but it does not identify opening a cardboard box as the bottleneck in an otherwise simulatable box-handling task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they have a good case when it comes to tasks where the physics are difficult to simulate accurately. For locomotion, we’re relatively lucky: you have rigid bodies, motors, and contact with the ground, and you can get a useful approximation of those things. You don’t need the simulation to be perfect for the policy to transfer.

But if you’re manipulating cloth, or interacting with something soft, it becomes much harder to build that simulation. Then you can reasonably ask whether the effort of building and tuning the simulator is greater than the effort of collecting experience on the real robot.

And ultimately, you care about performance in the real world. If there’s some effect your simulator doesn’t capture, training longer in simulation won’t necessarily solve it. So I think there’s a strong argument for using real-world experience, especially to improve a policy after you’ve trained it in simulation. The question is how much of the learning you need to do there.

r001.rationale: The response cites cloth or soft-object manipulation as difficult to simulate, but does not identify opening a cardboard box as the bottleneck in an otherwise largely simulatable box-handling task.
